newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OTC products gain ground vs listed derivatives-BIS.
newsitem.headline: OTC products gain ground vs listed derivatives-BIS.

text.p: Over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives activity is growing faster than volume in exchange-traded instruments, and the trend is likely to continue, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said.

BIS, in its third-quarter report, said that business in OTC products continued to be buoyant, and also said there was "increasing divergence between the pace of activity in OTC and exchange-traded markets."
As OTC products such as interest rate swaps gain in volume outstanding, standardised contracts traded on futures exchanges have tended to be relatively steady.

"With OTC and exchange-traded markets being influenced by similar financial environments, this divergence probably reflects the fact that, following a period of intensive and extensive development, exchange-traded instruments are reaching the mature stage of their life cycle," BIS said.

According to BIS, a continuation of the trend means that futures and options exchanges will see further pressure to lower their transaction costs and consolidate market share in order to compete with the OTC market.
BIS also said its hypothesis appeared supported by evidence showing that U.S. banks are making less active use of futures markets but are further increasing their OTC positions.
A factor favouring growth of OTC products has been the recent spate of bank mergers and acquisitions, resulting in larger derivatives portfolios held by the newly-joined, larger institutions.
The larger the derivatives portfolio held by the bank, the more opportunity it has to offset risk internally, as opposed to using exchange-listed products.
The growth in OTC activity reflected longer-term trends, including emergence of "an active and liquid interbank market," BIS said.

Further factors included the fact that financial market participants, especially institutional investors, were making more widespread use of derivatives. BIS also cited as factors the development of risk reduction techniques, improved credit evaluation methods, increasing standardisation within the OTC market, and creation of increasingly sophisticated risk management tools.
The trend was particularly apparent in interest rate products, BIS said.

The BIS noted data collected by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) showed total notional principal value of outstanding interest rate swaps rose 39 percent to $8.70 trillion at the end of 1995 from $6.24 trillion at end of 1994. The value of exchange-traded interest rate futures and options rose by only three percent to $8.61 trillion from $8.4 trllion in the same period.
"The high level of global liquidity and the improvement of credit quality of core participants appear to have been supportive of the market's expansion," BIS said.
"In addition, bull market conditions spurred fixed income issuance and therefore probably generated a higher volume of swap-related business," BIS said.
It also said the share of interbank swap business has risen to 57 percent at the end of 1995 from 51 percent at end-1994, and increased from only 32 percent in 1987.

BIS said that swaps "have played an instrumental role in the competitive strategy of commercial banks, enabling them to garner new sources of income and to maintain their presence at the core of the financial system at a time when capital markets represent a growing challenge to traditional lending." -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
